(b) Data Preparation¶

(i) Research what types of techniques are usually used¶

Common techniques for dealing with missing values include dropping rows or columns with missing values, filling the missing values with zero (or another constant), filling with the mean, median, or mode, using an algorithm that handles missing values natively such as XGBoost, or predicting the missing value from the other features with a model like linear regression or KNN. As stated in the assignment, dropping rows is not viable here since there are so many missing values. I have chosen to use median imputation since features have large outliers, so the median accounts for that and is a better fill value than the mean. The training set is filled with training-set medians and the test set with its own medians, since in the real world a deployed model would only be able to see the new data it's predicting on.

Looking at the scatter plots and box plots without any transformation, I am not able to draw any conclusions about the features. A few extreme outliers (one truck with cf_000 around 8.6 × 10⁹) stretch the axes so far that all the other trucks collapse onto the same line, so class 0 and class 1 look identical. So I also tried a log transformation (log(1 + x), with the +1 so zeros are accounted for), which spreads the data out. With this there is more meaning: for cf_000, class 0 has a median of about 0 while class 1 has a median of about 2; co_000 and ad_000 sit higher and tighter for class 1; and ay_009 is non-zero far more often for class 1. However, some features still look the same in both classes (for example ch_000), and even the ones that differ still have heavy overlap. So looking at these features alone, one cannot classify which class a truck falls into. The scatter plots are helpful for finding which features could be worth looking at, but they do not say whether a feature is significant. For that I would need a fitted model tested on held-out data, to see what the features contribute together.

(c) Train a random forest¶

In [8]:
def evaluate_model(model, title):
    pred_train = model.predict(x_train)
    pred_test = model.predict(x_test)
    prob_train = model.predict_proba(x_train)[:, 1]
    prob_test = model.predict_proba(x_test)[:, 1]

    print("Training confusion matrix:\n", confusion_matrix(y_train, pred_train))
    print("Test confusion matrix:\n", confusion_matrix(y_test, pred_test))
    print("Misclassification rate (train, test):", 1 - accuracy_score(y_train, pred_train), 1 - accuracy_score(y_test, pred_test))
    print("AUC (train, test):", roc_auc_score(y_train, prob_train), roc_auc_score(y_test, prob_test))

    fpr_train, tpr_train, _ = roc_curve(y_train, prob_train)
    fpr_test, tpr_test, _ = roc_curve(y_test, prob_test)
    plt.figure(figsize=(4, 4))
    plt.plot(fpr_train, tpr_train, color="#FFCC00", label="Training")
    plt.plot(fpr_test, tpr_test, color="#990000", label="Test")
    plt.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], linestyle="--", color="grey")
    plt.xlabel("FPR")
    plt.ylabel("TPR")
    plt.title(title)
    plt.legend()
    plt.show()

AUC (train, test): 1.0 0.9967202986666668

The out of bag (OOB) error estimate for the random forest is 0.58%, while the test error is 0.77%. The OOB estimate, which is slightly more optimistic, is calculated from only the training set by predicting each observation using only the trees whose bootstrap sample did not include it, similar to leave one out cross validation. Overall, the OOB error is close to the test error, so it can be said to be a reasonable replacement for a held out test set. Also, the training AUC is 1 and the training misclassification rate is 0, which tracks since the training data is fit perfectly by the random forest. Additionally, test AUC is 0.997 with 20 false positives and 103 false negatives, meaning 72.5% recall for the positive class (extreme class imbalance).

(d) Research class imbalance in random forest¶

Random forests can address class imbalance in two places: inside the forest itself, or in the data before training. Inside the forest, two methods were proposed by Chen, Liaw and Breiman (2004). The first is the balanced random forest, where each tree is grown from a bootstrap sample of the minority class together with an equally sized sample from the majority class, so each tree sees balanced data while the forest as a whole still uses all of the observations. The second is the weighted random forest, which gives the smaller class a larger weight that enters both the Gini criterion for splits and the weighted majority vote at the terminal nodes, so this is the more cost-sensitive approach. Chen et al. (2004) found both did better than other techniques such as SMOTE on imbalanced data, with no clear winner between the two. The weighted random forest can be implemented in scikit-learn through the class_weight parameter, set to “balanced” or “balanced_subsample” (scikit-learn developers, 2025). Addressing the imbalance through the data instead works by down-sampling the majority class, up-sampling the minority class with replacement, or generating synthetic minority observations with SMOTE (He & Garcia, 2009).

References

Chen, C., Liaw, A., & Breiman, L. (2004). Using random forest to learn imbalanced data (Technical Report No. 666). Department of Statistics, University of California, Berkeley. https://statistics.berkeley.edu/sites/default/files/tech-reports/666.pdf

He, H., & Garcia, E. A. (2009). Learning from imbalanced data. IEEE Transactions on Knowledge and Data Engineering, 21(9), 1263–1284. https://doi.org/10.1109/TKDE.2008.239

scikit-learn developers. (2025). sklearn.ensemble.RandomForestClassifier. https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.ensemble.RandomForestClassifier.html

                                      random_state=1106, n_jobs=-1)
rf_bal_model.fit(x_train, y_train)
print("OOB error:", 1 - rf_bal_model.oob_score_)
evaluate_model(rf_bal_model, "ROC Curves Balanced RF: Training vs Test")

OOB error: 0.007600000000000051
Training confusion matrix:
 [[59000     0]
 [    0  1000]]
Test confusion matrix:
 [[15609    16]
 [  158   217]]
Misclassification rate (train, test): 0.0 0.010874999999999968
AUC (train, test): 0.9999999999999999 0.9943282346666665

Using class_weight="balanced_subsample", the OOB error estimate for the weighted random forest is 0.76% and the test error is 1.09%, versus 0.58% and 0.77% in part c, so both went up. The training AUC is still 1 and the training misclassification rate is still 0, which tracks since the trees are grown until every leaf is pure. Test AUC is 0.994 compared to 0.997 before, so almost the same ranking ability. However, the test confusion matrix now has 16 false positives and 158 false negatives, meaning recall on the positive class dropped from 72.5% to 57.9%. So the weighting did not actually help the minority class here. This is because the trees are fully grown, so every leaf contains only negatives or only positives, and the weights do not affect the vote since a leaf can only vote for the one class it contains. The weights only change which splits are chosen while growing the trees, and in this case that reshuffling made the positive class predictions worse. To see a benefit from the weighting, the decision threshold would also need to be lowered from 0.5, or a method that changes the data each tree sees (like the balanced random forest) would need to be used instead.

Using SMOTE inside each of the CV folds, the best α was 0.1, with a CV misclassification error of 0.625%, similar to but slightly better than the test error of 0.781%. Compared to part e, where the test error was 0.638%, SMOTE adds a small amount of overall error. However, SMOTE made the positive class much better: recall went from 77.1% to 85.3%, so 55 false negatives versus 86. False positives did not improve, they increased from 16 to 70. This is expected when you oversample the minority class, since the model is trained to flag positives more readily. As stated in the problem set, a false negative (missing a faulty truck) is far more costly than a false positive (an unnecessary check), so this is a better trade-off.

2. ISLR 6.6.3¶

a) iv; steadily decreases: As s increases the constraint on the coefficients loosens (at s = 0 they are all forced to 0, and larger s lets them grow), so every model that was allowed before is still allowed and new, more complex ones are too. Therefore the model that best fits the training data has error ≤ the previous one, so the training RSS steadily decreases until it reaches the least squares value. b) ii; U shape: As the model becomes more flexible it is improving at first, so test RSS goes down. But once it gets to the point where it is overfitting, test RSS goes back up, because the model has learned to fit the training data rather than the pattern that carries over to the test data. c) iii; steadily increases: As the model becomes more flexible, variance increases, since the fit depends more on the specific training sample it was given. d) iv; steadily decreases: As the model becomes more flexible, bias goes down, since the constraint is loosened and the model can get closer to the true function on average. e) v; remains constant: Irreducible error is error you cannot change because it comes from the data (Var(ε)), not from the model. Making the model more flexible does not impact it.

3. ISLR 6.6.5¶

With $x_{11} = x_{12} = a$, $x_{21} = x_{22} = -a$ (from $x_{11} + x_{21} = 0$), $y_2 = -y_1$:

a)

$$\min_{\beta_1, \beta_2} \; (y_1 - \beta_1 x_{11} - \beta_2 x_{12})^2 + (y_2 - \beta_1 x_{21} - \beta_2 x_{22})^2 + \lambda(\beta_1^2 + \beta_2^2).$$

b) Once plugging in the given values we get:

$$(y_1 - a(\beta_1 + \beta_2))^2 + (y_2 + a(\beta_1 + \beta_2))^2 + \lambda(\beta_1^2 + \beta_2^2).$$

Since the two predictors are identical, $\beta_1$ and $\beta_2$ only ever appear in the RSS through their sum, so let $s = \beta_1 + \beta_2$. For a fixed $s$, the RSS terms $(y_1 - as)^2 + (y_2 + as)^2$ are constant regardless of how $s$ is split between $\beta_1$ and $\beta_2$, so the only part of the objective that still depends on the split is the penalty. Therefore, to find the best split for a given $s$, we only need to minimise $\beta_1^2 + \beta_2^2$ subject to $\beta_1 + \beta_2 = s$. Substituting $\beta_2 = s - \beta_1$ and differentiating with respect to $\beta_1$:

$$2\beta_1 - 2(s - \beta_1) = 0 \iff \beta_1 = \tfrac{s}{2} = \beta_2$$

We find the 2nd derivative is $4 > 0$, so this is the minimum. Hence at the ridge optimum $\hat\beta_1 = \hat\beta_2$.

c) For the lasso, we would minimize over $\beta_1$ and $\beta_2$:

$$\min_{\beta_1, \beta_2} \; (y_1 - \beta_1 x_{11} - \beta_2 x_{12})^2 + (y_2 - \beta_1 x_{21} - \beta_2 x_{22})^2 + \lambda(|\beta_1| + |\beta_2|).$$

d) Plugging in the given values as in (b) and letting $s = \beta_1 + \beta_2$:

$$(y_1 - as)^2 + (y_2 + as)^2 + \lambda(|\beta_1| + |\beta_2|)$$

Since the RSS terms are constant and do not depend on how $s$ is split, we are now minimising the penalty $|\beta_1| + |\beta_2|$ subject to $\beta_1 + \beta_2 = s$. By the triangle inequality,

$$|\beta_1| + |\beta_2| \geq |\beta_1 + \beta_2| = |s|,$$

with equality iff $\beta_1$ and $\beta_2$ have the same sign (or one is zero). So any pair with $\beta_1 + \beta_2 = s$ and matching signs gives the same minimum penalty $|s|$, meaning there is no single best split. If we call the optimal sum $\hat s$, the lasso solutions are

$$\{(\beta_1, \beta_2) : \beta_1 + \beta_2 = \hat s, \; \beta_1 \text{ and } \beta_2 \text{ of the same sign as } \hat s\},$$

i.e. the whole line segment from $(\hat s, 0)$ to $(0, \hat s)$. This proves that the lasso coefficients are not unique.

4. ISLR 8.4.5¶

The two methods disagree in this case. Calculating by majority vote, 6 of the 10 trees give P(Red | X) > 0.5 and 4 give P(Red | X) < 0.5, so Red has 6 votes and Green has 4, meaning the final classification is Red since it has more votes. However, using average probability, the total of the 10 estimates is 4.5, and dividing by 10 gives 0.45, which is less than 0.5, so the classification under this technique is Green. The disagreement happens because the trees giving 0.1, 0.15 and 0.2 are very confidently predicting Green, whereas the ones predicting Red (anything above 0.5) are closer to 0.5 than to 1. So the average ends up below 0.5 even though Red has the majority.

5. ISLR 9.7.3¶

(a)¶

In [13]:
feature1 = np.array([3, 2, 4, 1, 2, 4, 4])
feature2 = np.array([4, 2, 4, 4, 1, 3, 1])
colors = np.array(["red"] * 4 + ["blue"] * 3)

plt.figure(figsize=(3, 3))
plt.scatter(feature1, feature2, c=colors, s=100, edgecolor="black")
plt.xlim(0, 5)
plt.ylim(0, 5)
plt.xlabel("Feature 1")
plt.ylabel("Feature 2")
plt.title("Scatter of the 7 Observations")
plt.show()

(b)¶

In [14]:
line_x = np.array([0, 5])

plt.figure(figsize=(4, 4))
plt.scatter(feature1, feature2, c=colors, s=50, edgecolor="black")
plt.plot(line_x, line_x - 0.5, color="black", label="0.5 - X1 + X2 = 0")
plt.plot(line_x, line_x, color="grey", linestyle="--", label="Margin")
plt.plot(line_x, line_x - 1, color="grey", linestyle="--")
plt.scatter([2, 4, 2, 4], [2, 4, 1, 3], s=150, facecolor="none", edgecolor="black", label="Support vectors")
plt.xlim(0, 5)
plt.ylim(0, 5)
plt.xlabel("Feature 1")
plt.ylabel("Feature 2")
plt.title("Optimal Separating Hyperplane")
plt.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=7)
plt.show()

We see that the optimal hyperplane separating the classes is 0.5 − X₁ + X₂ = 0 (i.e. X₂ = X₁ − 0.5), since it lies halfway between the line X₂ = X₁ through the closest red points and the line X₂ = X₁ − 1 through the closest blue points.

(c)¶

If 0.5 − X₁ + X₂ > 0, then it is classified as Red; if < 0, then Blue.

(d)¶

The margin is found by taking the hyperplane and finding the perpendicular distance to the dashed lines, i.e. where the nearest points are. This can be calculated as |0.5 − X₁ + X₂| / √((−1)² + 1²) = 0.5/√2 ≈ 0.354.

(e)¶

The support vectors are observation 2, point (2, 2), and observation 3, point (4, 4), for Red. For Blue, they are observation 5, point (2, 1), and observation 6, point (4, 3). These are the points on the margin boundaries.

(f)¶

Plugging (4, 1) into the equation gives 0.5 − 4 + 1 = −2.5, which is well below the −0.5 of the blue support vectors. So it sits outside the margin and is therefore not a support vector. If we were to move observation 7 a bit, it would not change the hyperplane at all, because it would still stay outside the margin boundary at −0.5, and only the support vectors determine the maximal margin hyperplane.

(g)¶

In [15]:
plt.figure(figsize=(3, 3))
plt.scatter(feature1, feature2, c=colors, s=100, edgecolor="black")
plt.plot(line_x, line_x - 0.6, color="black")
plt.xlim(0, 5)
plt.ylim(0, 5)
plt.xlabel("Feature 1")
plt.ylabel("Feature 2")
plt.title("Non-Optimal Separating Hyperplane")
plt.show()

For this problem, any hyperplane c − X₁ + X₂ = 0 with 0 < c < 1 will separate the classes, since the red points on X₂ = X₁ give c > 0 and the blue points on X₂ = X₁ − 1 give c − 1 < 0. For the graph I chose c = 0.6, giving 0.6 − X₁ + X₂ = 0. This is 0.4 from the nearest blue points and 0.6 from the nearest red points, so it is slightly closer to the blue side and its margin is smaller than the optimal hyperplane’s.

(h)¶

plt.scatter(feature1, feature2, c=colors, s=100, edgecolor="black")
plt.scatter(5, 2, c="#FF6666", s=250, edgecolor="black", marker="*")
plt.xlim(0, 6)
plt.ylim(0, 6)
plt.xlabel("Feature 1")
plt.ylabel("Feature 2")
plt.title("Classes No Longer Separable")
plt.show()

I added a Red observation at (5, 2), shown as a star on the graph. Plugging it into the optimal hyperplane gives 0.5 − 5 + 2 = −2.5, so it falls on the Blue side, to the right of the blue points (4, 1) and (4, 3), which makes the two classes impossible to separate with a single straight line.
